question: What changes when a dance tune is played on an instrument that sounds slightly wrong?
intro: Death plays the fiddle in the Fourth’s scherzo: a solo violin tuned a whole tone high, answered twice by slow, rustic trios. Listen for the scherzo’s sting, which returns each time and has almost gone by the last page.

sections.label: Scherzo returns
sections.mNote: solo violin marked leidenschaftlich, orchestra louder than at the opening

sections.label: Trio II · Nicht eilen
sections.mNote: trio returns longer, with major-key digressions

sections.label: Last scherzo and close
sections.mNote: muted strings at ppp; the scherzo loses its sting

cues.title: A horn call, then the fiddle
cues.text: A solo horn plays a short call, then the solo violin enters “wie eine Fidel” — like a fiddle. Its strings are tuned a whole tone high, so the tone is thin and edgy. The score asks the soloist to stand out strongly and to play without a mute.
cues.evidence: Full score (IMSLP70999), PDF p. 49: horn solo in the opening bars; the solo-violin entry is marked “wie eine Fidel” and “immer stark hervortretend und ohne Dämpfer”. In the report, relative level rises at 0:05 and attack density reaches 3.8 per second by 0:10. The entry bar is not aligned to the recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Friend Hein
cues.text: Mahler first headed this movement with a line about Death scraping his fiddle bizarrely and leading us up to heaven. “Freund Hein” is the German folk name for Death, often pictured as a skeleton fiddler in the Totentanz, the dance of death.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s movement page quotes the original heading and explains Freund Hein and the Totentanz: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-2-in-gemachlicher-bewegung/

cues.title: A brief major-key respite
cues.text: For a few bars the minor-key fiddling gives way to a lighter patch in the major, and the oboe chords recall the first movement while pointing ahead to the finale. The sting returns almost at once.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s guide describes a brief move into the major mode, with oboe chords that recall the first movement and anticipate the finale: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . In the report, key estimates read C major at 0:40 and 0:45 (r 0.75, 0.72) while attack density falls to 1.0 per second at 0:45. No individual player is identified.

cues.title: A dry accompaniment
cues.text: Around the fiddle, Mahler asks for muted strings, pizzicato and, later, col legno — tapping the strings with the wood of the bow. Listen for these dry, hollow sounds beneath the violin’s shrill tune.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 49–53 and 58: “mit Dämpfer”, “pizz.” and “col legno” are printed in the scherzo sections. Basinger also lists mutes and col legno among the scherzo’s colours: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: the scherzo is active at 0:50–1:10, with attack density 3.0–4.6 per second at −20.0 to −16.9 dB and brightness up to 2736 Hz at 0:50. Col legno is a later score colour (PDF p. 58), not an entrance detected at 0:58; this cue describes the score’s colours, not a timed event.

cues.title: Trio I: do not hurry
cues.text: At rehearsal 3 the marking is “Nicht eilen” — do not hurry — and the key signature drops to one flat, F major. The first trio is a Ländler, a slow rustic dance led by woodwinds, with the pastoral calm the scherzo lacks.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 54: rehearsal 3, “Nicht eilen”, a one-flat signature in the flutes and oboes (one sharp in the B♭ clarinets), then “Etwas gemächlicher” a few bars later. In the report there is a structural boundary at 1:16 (novelty 0.61), brightness falls from 2259 Hz at 1:10 to 1136 Hz at 1:15, and key estimates lean to F major and F minor from 1:35 (r 0.61–0.75). Basinger describes the trios as ländler-like and pastoral.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Woodwinds over held horns
cues.text: Oboes and clarinets pass the trio’s tune between them over sustained horns and plucked basses. The violins add soft special effects: playing over the fingerboard and on the G string alone.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 55: violins marked “Griffbrett” and “G-Saite”, horns sustained, pizzicato in cellos and basses, woodwind staves active. In the report brightness stays between 1002 and 1154 Hz at 1:20–1:30 and attacks are 1–2 per second. The passage is placed approximately by page proportion.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A leaf for Arnold Rosé
cues.text: On 11 January 1902, the day before the Vienna performance, Mahler gave the violinist Arnold Rosé a manuscript leaf of this solo. In that draft the violin is tuned a half-tone high; the printed score asks for a whole tone.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation’s movement page describes the manuscript: the solo violin part is noted “um einen halben Ton höher gestimmt”, the leaf is dated 11 January 1902 and was given to Arnold Rosé the day before the Vienna premiere, and the final version is tuned a whole tone higher: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-2-in-gemachlicher-bewegung/ . The Vienna concert date, 12 January 1902, is on the work’s history page.

cues.title: The trio dies away
cues.text: The first trio stays in F major to the end. Cellos and basses murmur, horns hold soft notes, and the marking is “morendo” as the dynamic sinks to pppp before the scherzo breaks in.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 56–57: rehearsal 4, one-flat signature kept, “morendo” in the low strings and a final “pppp”. In the report relative level is −22.6 dB at 2:00 and attack density is 0.2–0.4 per second from 2:15 to 2:25, with brightness 905 Hz at 2:20.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fiddler returns
cues.text: At the second “Tempo I”, rehearsal 5, the scherzo is back. The solo violin is marked “leidenschaftlich” — passionately — and the orchestra is louder than at the opening.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 58: rehearsal 5, “Tempo I.”, solo violin marked “leidenschaftlich” with ff. In the report the strongest boundary is 2:32 (novelty 1.00), attack density rises from 0.4 per second at 2:25 to 1.4 at 2:30 and 1.6 at 2:35, and relative level rises from −17.9 dB at 2:35 to −11 dB from 2:40.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The loudest stretch
cues.text: The orchestra reaches the movement’s highest relative level here, peaking near 2:55. The scordatura violin is written to project over the whole band; listen for its edge above the mass.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is about −11 dB at 2:40–2:50 and −8.9 dB at 2:55, the loudest five-second window in the file. The solo violin is marked “immer stark hervortretend” on PDF p. 49 of the full score. The report does not separate instruments.

cues.title: Böcklin’s fiddling skeleton
cues.text: Alma Mahler later claimed that Arnold Böcklin’s 1872 Self-Portrait with Death Fiddling inspired this scherzo. She and Mahler had not yet met when he composed it, though he admired Böcklin’s work.
cues.evidence: Basinger records Alma’s claim and notes that the couple had not met when the music was composed, and that Mahler admired Böcklin: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . The Mahler Foundation page also reports Alma’s account: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-4/symphony-no-4-movement-2-in-gemachlicher-bewegung/

cues.title: A pause in the argument
cues.text: After the first great surge the attacks thin out. From about 3:15 the music is sparse and settles towards C major, and the scherzo takes a breath before it gathers again.
cues.evidence: Report: attack density is 0.6 per second at 3:15 and 0.8 at 3:20, relative level eases to about −17 dB, and key estimates read C major (r 0.73) at 3:15; level and attacks then rise from 3:25.

cues.title: A second surge
cues.text: The sound builds again to a second peak between 3:30 and 3:45, almost as loud as the first and busier: about three to five attacks a second by 3:45.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −9.5 dB at 3:30, −9.7 at 3:35, −10.7 at 3:40 and −10.5 at 3:45; attack density is 3.6, 2.4, 2.8 and 4.6 per second in those windows. Four of the five loudest windows lie in 3:30–3:45.

cues.title: Walter’s title for it
cues.text: On 5 December 1901 Bruno Walter, at Mahler’s request, described the symphony for the scholar Ludwig Schiedermair. This movement, he wrote, might be called “Freund Hein Strikes Up the Dance”: his playing “sends us up into Heaven”.
cues.evidence: Basinger quotes Walter’s reply of 5 December 1901 and the circumstances of the request: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: Trio II: Nicht eilen again
cues.text: At rehearsal 8 comes “Nicht eilen” again, and the second trio begins. The pace relaxes and attacks thin out; woodwinds, horns and trumpets lead, with glockenspiel and harp adding points of light. It is longer and more varied than the first.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 65: rehearsal 8, “Nicht eilen”, with wind, horn, trumpet, glockenspiel and harp staves active. In the report relative level falls from −13.1 dB at 4:35 to −20.6 dB at 4:40 and attack density drops to 0.6 per second at 4:45.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: More leisurely still
cues.text: At rehearsal 9 the marking is “Wieder gemächlicher” — again more leisurely. From 5:05 the music retreats in stages, and between 5:25 and 5:45 attacks almost disappear. Listen to how little the music needs.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 66: rehearsal 9, “Wieder gemächlicher”. Report: level falls from −16.6 dB at 5:05 to −18.3 dB at 5:10 and −21.5 dB at 5:15, with a brief 1.6 attacks per second at 5:20; from 5:25 to 5:45 attack density is 0.0–0.4 per second at −23.0 to −21.7 dB. The rehearsal figure is placed by page proportion.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A late addition
cues.text: Mahler’s proof corrections doubled the double basses with contrabassoon in bars 246–51 of this movement. The engraved plate had no room for another staff, so the published score labels one line “Ctrfag. u. Cb. unisono”.
cues.evidence: Paul Banks’s catalogue of the Fourth Symphony’s printed sources describes the revision and the engraver’s solution: http://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/Symph4/Symph4prints.htm . The label is visible in the full score, PDF p. 69. The passage is placed approximately by page proportion.

cues.title: Spreading out in D major
cues.text: At rehearsal 11, “Sich noch mehr ausbreitend” — spreading out still more — two sharps appear. The orchestra opens into a warm D major; the violins slide between notes while the harp arpeggiates.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 69: rehearsal 11, “Sich noch mehr ausbreitend”, two-sharp signature, “gliss.” in the violins and harp figures. In the report there are boundaries at 5:46 (0.55) and 5:52 (0.79) and key estimates read D major from 5:55 (r 0.72–0.79).
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The trio swells and holds
cues.text: Around 6:15 the second trio reaches its loudest point. Soon after, at rehearsal 12, Mahler marks “Gehalten” — held — and then asks for a gradual return to the first tempo.
cues.evidence: Report: relative level is −11.3 dB at 6:15 and −13.1 dB at 6:20, then falls to −22.7 dB by 6:30. Full score, PDF p. 71: “Gehalten” at rehearsal 12 and “Allmählich zur ersten Bewegung zurückkehrend”. The two are placed by page proportion and the report, not aligned bar by bar.

cues.title: The scherzo intrudes
cues.text: From about 6:35 the attacks climb from almost none to three a second and the key estimates turn to G minor. Scherzo ideas push into the trio before its tune comes back.
cues.evidence: Report: attack density is 0.0 at 6:25, 2.0 at 6:40 and 3.2 at 6:50; key estimates read G minor (r 0.67–0.72) from 6:25. Basinger notes that ideas from the scherzo eventually intrude upon the trio: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

cues.title: The last scherzo opens softly
cues.text: At the final “Tempo I”, rehearsal 13, the strings are muted and marked ppp, with plucked cellos and basses beneath. Against this soft background the first solo-violin staff plays loud pizzicato notes. Basinger hears the closing scherzo as gentler than before.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 73: rehearsal 13, “Tempo I.”, muted strings marked ppp, cellos and basses pizzicato; the first solo-violin staff has pizzicato notes marked ff or louder (read as fff on the scan) while the second solo staff is muted at pp. Basinger describes the closing scherzo as beginning with a major-mode interlude and as having lost its sting: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/ . Report: boundary at 7:26 (novelty 0.54), attack density 0.6–0.8 per second at 7:30–7:35.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A glint of high percussion
cues.text: Around 7:55 the sound brightens sharply: trills in the high woodwinds with triangle, harp and tam-tam glitter over the muted strings, then the texture thins again.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 74–75: rehearsal 14 with triangle, harp, tam-tam, bass drum and woodwind trills over strings marked “immer mit Dämpfer”. Report: spectral brightness reaches 2899 Hz at 7:55, the highest of the movement, at −16.7 dB.

cues.title: Sliding into silence
cues.text: On the last page the cellos slide on the C string while the clarinets fade “morendo”. The movement ends as it began, lightly, and without the weight a minor-key scherzo might suggest.
cues.evidence: Full score, PDF p. 77 (printed p. 303): “sempre gliss. auf der C-Saite” in the cellos and “morendo” in the clarinets. Report: relative level falls from −16.1 dB at 8:10 to −27.7 dB at 8:25 and −68.1 dB at 8:30, near-silence.

transitions.title: One flat, and the pace relaxes
transitions.how: The scherzo’s C-minor fiddling gives way to a slower, plainer dance. At rehearsal 3 the three flats of the signature drop to one, F major, and Mahler writes “Nicht eilen”, then “Etwas gemächlicher” a few bars later. The orchestration changes from the fiddle, muted strings and dry accents to woodwinds with trills, held horns and plucked basses; the violins now colour the texture with special effects such as “Griffbrett” and “G-Saite”. The join is made by pace and colour, not by a bridging passage.
transitions.evidence: Full score (IMSLP70999), PDF pp. 54–55: rehearsal 3 with “Nicht eilen” and “Etwas gemächlicher”, a new one-flat signature in the flutes and oboes, “Griffbrett” and “G-Saite”. Report: boundary at 1:16 (novelty 0.61) and brightness falling from 2259 Hz at 1:10 to 1136 Hz at 1:15. The exact bar of the join is not aligned.

transitions.title: Pppp, then the fiddle returns
transitions.how: The first trio does not close with a cadence into the scherzo. It dwindles in F major: cellos and basses murmur “morendo”, horns hold soft notes and the dynamic is marked down to pppp. Then rehearsal 5 simply says “Tempo I”: three flats return, the solo violin plays “leidenschaftlich”, and the whole orchestra takes up the scherzo at greater volume than at the opening. The contrast between near-silence and the fiddle’s entry carries the join.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 57–58: one-flat signature, “morendo” and pppp, then rehearsal 5 “Tempo I.” and “leidenschaftlich”. Report: sparse writing at 2:15–2:25 (0.2–0.4 attacks per second), strongest boundary at 2:32 (novelty 1.00) and relative level rising to −11 dB by 2:40.

transitions.title: Trills run out; the trio relaxes
transitions.how: The returned scherzo ends in a burst of woodwind trills and a “lustig” horn call over busy strings. At rehearsal 8 Mahler writes “Nicht eilen” again and the music relaxes into the second trio: woodwinds and trumpets lead, glockenspiel and harp add light touches, and a third bassoon is told to take the contrabassoon. The trills carry across the join, but their role changes from nervous decoration to pastoral colour.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 64–65: closing page with trills and the “lustig” horn marking, then rehearsal 8 “Nicht eilen” and the instruction that the third bassoon takes the contrabassoon. Report: relative level falls from −13.1 dB at 4:35 to −20.6 dB at 4:40 and attacks fall to 0.6 per second at 4:45.

transitions.title: Held back, then softly home
transitions.how: The second trio peaks, then Mahler writes “Gehalten” (rehearsal 12) and “Allmählich zur ersten Bewegung zurückkehrend” — gradually returning to the first tempo — while scherzo figures press into the trio, the attacks multiplying as the key estimates darken towards G minor. At rehearsal 13 “Tempo I” arrives not with a bang but with muted strings at ppp over plucked cellos and basses. This long retransition lets the return arrive quietly; Basinger hears the closing scherzo as having lost its sting.
transitions.evidence: Full score, PDF pp. 71 and 73: “Gehalten” at rehearsal 12, “Allmählich zur ersten Bewegung zurückkehrend”, and rehearsal 13 “Tempo I.” with muted ppp strings and pizzicato cellos and basses. Report: attack density climbs from 0.0 at 6:25 to 3.2 per second at 6:50 with G minor estimates, then boundary at 7:26 (novelty 0.54). Basinger describes the quiet closing scherzo: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/05/mahler-4-listening-guide/

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 4, II. In gemächlicher Bewegung, full score (IMSLP70999)
source.locator: PDF pp. 49–77 (printed pp. 275–303), rehearsal figures 1–14; changes are placed at the recording’s existing passage anchors and are approximate.

timeline.note: A solo horn call opens, with soft woodwind trills; the scordatura violin enters “wie eine Fidel” above muted violas and cellos.
Violins, violas and basses gather around the fiddle in muted and pizzicato figures, with timpani and low winds.
Woodwinds lead the first trio over held horns and plucked basses; trills and harp add light.
Cellos and basses murmur beneath held horns as the trio dies away to pppp.
The scherzo returns: the solo violin plays passionately over horns, harp, bass drum and strings that tap col legno.
The full band joins the fiddle at the movement’s loudest stretch, with muted trumpet, cymbals and timpani.
Muted horns and trumpets and a ringing glockenspiel punctuate the busy strings.
The second trio relaxes: flutes, piccolos and oboes trill, trumpets and horns sustain, glockenspiel and harp add light.
D major opens out: clarinets sing, violins slide, harp arpeggiates and the contrabassoon doubles the basses.
The trio swells and holds, with piccolo and flutes above divided strings, before the tempo begins to return.
Muted violins and violas play at ppp over plucked cellos and basses, with held horns, harp and piccolo.
Woodwind trills, triangle, harp and tam-tam glitter over muted strings.
Cellos slide on the C string over soft basses as the clarinets fade “morendo”.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
